event_overview.title: About Iran War
event_overview.subject: Iran War
event_overview.summary: The Iran War refers here to the 2026 regional armed conflict that began with U.S. and Israeli military action against Iran and was followed by Iranian attacks and retaliation affecting neighboring states and maritime traffic. The Strait of Hormuz became a central theater because attacks, restrictions and military operations there disrupted commercial shipping while ceasefire and diplomatic efforts remained fragile.

facts.label: Start and principal belligerents
facts.value: The United Nations Secretary-General described the escalation as beginning on 28 February 2026, with U.S. and Israeli use of force against Iran followed by Iranian attacks across the region. In its formal notification to the Security Council, the United States said it had commenced combat operations that day in cooperation with Israel.

facts.label: Regional reach
facts.value: The conflict was not confined to Iran: the Secretary-General identified subsequent Iranian attacks affecting Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

facts.label: Stated U.S. rationale and disputed legal
facts.value: The United States told the Security Council that its operations were undertaken to protect U.S. forces, maritime commerce through the Strait of Hormuz, and regional partners, invoking self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter. Iran has disputed that characterization and described the U.S.-Israeli action as aggression, illustrating that the conflict's legal and political framing is contested.

facts.label: Maritime dimension
facts.value: The International Maritime Organization identifies the Strait of Hormuz as a key shipping route with an IMO-adopted traffic-separation scheme, proposed by Iran and Oman in 1968, intended to reduce collisions and improve safety. As of 15 October 2026, IMO described an ongoing situation affecting roughly 20,000 seafarers, port workers and offshore crews in the region.

facts.label: International response
facts.value: The Security Council adopted resolution 2817 (2026) on 11 March 2026; the meeting record says it required Iran to cease attacks against specified Gulf states and Jordan and emphasized respect for navigational rights and freedoms of merchant and commercial vessels under international law.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers a short sequence of late-July 2026 escalation, congressional war-powers activity, Houthi-linked developments and ceasefire talks; it does not provide a complete account of the conflict's origins, all military operations, humanitarian effects or subsequent diplomacy.

event_overview.title: About Protests in France
event_overview.subject: Protests in France
event_overview.summary: The event is a wave of nationwide demonstrations in France that grew from a student-led movement over conditions in secondary schools into broader protests over living costs, inflation and public services. Large peaceful marches on October 17, 2026 were accompanied in some locations by clashes, vandalism and looting, prompting local security measures and a national political response.

facts.label: Origins and stated grievances
facts.value: Reporting describes the movement as beginning with high-school student protests in late September 2026 over lycée conditions, then expanding to include concerns about the cost of living, inflation and public services.

facts.label: Major nationwide mobilization
facts.value: The principal nationwide demonstrations took place on Saturday, October 17, 2026; reporting distinguished the large peaceful marches from violent incidents that occurred on their margins in several cities.

facts.label: Participants and organization
facts.value: This is a decentralized social protest movement rather than a single event run by one organizer: participants reported across coverage include students, trade unions, Yellow Vest supporters, workers in several sectors and political activists.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Demonstrations and subsequent disorder were reported across France, including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux; the event therefore involves both national political issues and locally imposed public-order measures.

facts.label: Legal framework for public demonstration
facts.value: French law requires prior declaration for processions, parades and other demonstrations on public roads. In general, organizers file between three and 15 clear days in advance with the relevant mayor or prefecture; authorities may prohibit a planned demonstration when they judge it likely to disturb public order.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the immediate aftermath and official responses on October 18-19, 2026, including disruption in Paris and Marseille; it does not attempt to catalogue every protest, participant group, injury, arrest, damage claim or later legal proceeding.

event_overview.title: About Protests in France
event_overview.subject: Protests in France
event_overview.summary: The event is a wave of nationwide demonstrations in France that grew from a student-led movement over conditions in secondary schools into broader protests over living costs, inflation and public services. Large peaceful marches on October 17, 2026 were accompanied in some locations by clashes, vandalism and looting, prompting local security measures and a national political response.

facts.label: Origins and stated grievances
facts.value: Reporting describes the movement as beginning with high-school student protests in late September 2026 over lycée conditions, then expanding to include concerns about the cost of living, inflation and public services.

facts.label: Major nationwide mobilization
facts.value: The principal nationwide demonstrations took place on Saturday, October 17, 2026; reporting distinguished the large peaceful marches from violent incidents that occurred on their margins in several cities.

facts.label: Participants and organization
facts.value: This is a decentralized social protest movement rather than a single event run by one organizer: participants reported across coverage include students, trade unions, Yellow Vest supporters, workers in several sectors and political activists.

facts.label: Geographic scope
facts.value: Demonstrations and subsequent disorder were reported across France, including Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux; the event therefore involves both national political issues and locally imposed public-order measures.

facts.label: Legal framework for public demonstration
facts.value: French law requires prior declaration for processions, parades and other demonstrations on public roads. In general, organizers file between three and 15 clear days in advance with the relevant mayor or prefecture; authorities may prohibit a planned demonstration when they judge it likely to disturb public order.

event_overview.scope_note: The selected Muninn timeline covers the immediate aftermath and official responses on October 18-19, 2026, including disruption in Paris and Marseille; it does not attempt to catalogue every protest, participant group, injury, arrest, damage claim or later legal proceeding.
